title: Transitions
intro: Choose a word that shows how two ideas connect.

sections.heading: Read both sides first
body: Read the full ideas before and after the transition. Name their relationship: addition, contrast, cause, time order, or example.
Choose for that relationship, not for a sophisticated sound. However signals contrast; therefore signals a conclusion or result.

examples.text: The road was icy. Therefore, the bus ran late.
examples.label: icy road causes the delay — cause/effect fits

examples.text: The road was icy. However, the bus ran late.
examples.label: 'However' signals a contrast that isn't there — the delay follows from the ice

sections.tip: Cover the transition, read both sentences, name the relationship in plain words, then choose.

sections.heading: Transition words by category
body: Addition: also, furthermore, moreover, similarly, likewise. Contrast: however, but, yet, nevertheless, although. Cause/result: therefore, thus, consequently, so. Time: first, then, meanwhile, afterward. Example/emphasis: for example, for instance, indeed, in other words.

Check grammar as well as meaning. But and yet can join complete thoughts with a comma. Although makes its clause depend on another. However and therefore cannot join two complete thoughts with a comma alone; use a period or semicolon.

examples.text: Sales rose all spring. Furthermore, online orders doubled.
examples.label: addition — a second supporting point

examples.text: The plan looked perfect on paper. In practice, however, it failed.
examples.label: contrast — reality clashes with the plan, so 'however' fits

examples.text: Sales rose all spring. However, online orders doubled.
examples.label: 'However' promises a clash, but the second idea supports the first

sections.tip: Sort the four choices into addition, contrast, cause/effect, and sequence. The right bucket usually has only one choice in it.

sections.heading: Watch for the contrast trap and 'no transition'
body: Contrast requires a real turn, limitation, or surprise. Agreement or added support needs a different connection.
A transition may be unnecessary. Try DELETE, but keep the relationship clear and the sentence grammatical; shorter is not automatically better.

examples.text: She studied for weeks. As a result, she passed easily.
examples.label: studying causes passing — effect word fits

examples.text: She studied for weeks. For example, she passed easily.
examples.label: passing is not an example of studying

sections.tip: If the second idea fights the first, pick contrast. If it agrees, pick addition. If neither, consider dropping the transition.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: Compare the ideas, name their relationship, and eliminate choices with the wrong meaning. Then insert the remaining choice and check punctuation.
Do not guess from answer patterns. Similar transitions may differ in nuance or syntax; confirm which one fits the whole passage.
sections.tip: Synonyms cancel each other: two choices with the same meaning are both wrong. Eliminate them in one stroke.

check.stem: The factory cut its energy use in half last year. [[However,]] it reduced its water consumption.
check.explanation: Reducing water consumption is a second improvement that piles onto the energy savings, so the addition phrase 'In addition,' fits. 'However,' 'Nevertheless,' and 'In contrast' all signal a clash, but the two sentences agree.

check.stem: Heavy rain flooded the trail. [[Meanwhile,]] the hikers had to turn back.
check.explanation: The flooding caused the hikers to turn back, so the cause/effect phrase 'As a result,' is correct. 'Meanwhile' signals two separate things happening at the same time, 'For instance' introduces an example, and 'In other words' restates an idea; none of those matches cause and effect.

check.stem: First, let the dough rest for an hour. [[Therefore,]] roll it into thin sheets.
check.explanation: The two steps happen in order, so the sequence word 'Then,' is needed. 'Therefore' claims the resting causes the rolling, 'However' signals a clash between the steps, and 'For example' calls the rolling an illustration of the resting; none of those matches a step-by-step process.
